notes: Patent appeal stay application; Jacob LJ refused adjournment pending EPO opposition with full reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Machinery Developments v St Merryn: refuse stay of patent appeal pending EPO
key_facts: MDL and Pechiney succeeded in the Patents County Court on validity and infringement of patent 0,687,238 against St Merryn's M602 machine.
The EPO opposition division held the patent invalid for added subject matter in December 2004, with appeal likely to take four to five years.
Patentees sought to stay the pending Court of Appeal on infringement and validity until final EPO determination, offering to discharge injunctions and give wide undertakings.
The appeal was listed for three days in February 2005 and the patentees' principal stated reason was legal costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to adjourn/stay pending appeals from Patents County Court judgments on validity, infringement and a modified non-infringing machine.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the appeal will proceed and existing injunctions remain in force subject to the court's order.
enrichment.ratio: Unless EPO resolution is reasonably imminent, it is often unjust to stay English patent proceedings while opposition runs its course; prejudice from years of commercial uncertainty and cost delay outweighs a patentee's unparticularised costs concerns, following Beloit and Kimberly-Clark.
legal_issues: Whether pending EPO opposition proceedings justified staying the Court of Appeal
Whether undertakings to discharge injunctions and limit relief to royalties adequately protected defendants
Commercial prejudice from leaving a valid-and-infringed decision standing during lengthy EPO delay
Whether EPO issue-by-issue opposition procedure complies with Article 6 ECHR
linked_authorities: Beloit Technologies v Paper Machinery [1997] RPC 489

notes: Liquidator assignment challenge; Arden LJ restored application struck out without evidence on delay and dual-role points.

enrichment.short_title: Ultraframe v Rigby: set-aside of liquidator IP assignments not strike-out case
key_facts: Liquidator Mr Rigby sold Quickfit Conservatories' intellectual property and related claims to Mr Fielding and TBG for nominal sums in 2001 and 2003.
Ultraframe, a creditor and litigant against Fielding and TBG, applied under sections 167 and 168 to set aside the assignments more than three years after learning of the first two.
HHJ Maddocks struck out the application at a directions hearing without allowing Ultraframe to adduce evidence in reply to documents produced by the respondents.
Ultraframe contended the liquidator sold assets without seeking better offers and that the third assignment was worth far more than £8,000 given ongoing multi-million pound litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from strike-out of an application to reverse a liquidator's assignment decisions under the Insolvency Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the application is restored and directions will be made for its future conduct.
enrichment.ratio: An application under sections 167 and 168 has a real prospect of success where it alleges a liquidator sold company assets without considering better offers; delay and a creditor's dual litigation motivation are not knock-out points on strike-out, and the judge should not decide such issues without evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Ultraframe's challenge to Mr Rigby's assignments was an abuse of process
Application of the Re Edennote/Faryab test for interfering with a liquidator's decisions
Whether delay and Ultraframe's tactical litigation purpose barred relief
Procedural fairness where strike-out was sought at a directions hearing without evidence

notes: Composite workplace-stress guidance judgment covering six appeals; metadata names Hartman only.

enrichment.short_title: Workplace stress appeals: Hatton/Barber principles applied to six psychiatric injury claims
key_facts: The Court of Appeal heard six consecutively listed appeals on employer liability for psychiatric injury caused by workplace stress.
Despite Hatton v Sutherland and Barber v Somerset County Council, trial judges were still applying the principles inconsistently and hearings were often disproportionately long.
Four appeals were brought by employers and two by claimants across NHS, university, banking, newspaper, manufacturing and prison healthcare settings.
Outcomes varied: Hartman and Best employer appeals succeeded; Wheeldon, Moore and Melville employer appeals failed; Green claimant appeal failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal judgment disposing of six appeals from trial decisions on stress-at-work negligence claims.
enrichment.outcome: Hartman and Best allowed (claims dismissed); Wheeldon, Green, Moore and Melville dismissed, restoring or affirming findings of liability or non-liability according to each appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Liability for psychiatric injury at work depends on foreseeable injury from breach of duty, not stress alone; where an employer has foreseen a specific risk and devised adequate systems, failure to implement those systems can make injury foreseeable without requiring pre-event warning signs in the employee.
legal_issues: Application of Hatton foreseeability guidance to varied workplace stress facts
When occupational health services affect breach and foreseeability
Foreseeability where employers foresee class risk from traumatic incidents
Proportionality of trial length and damages assessment in stress claims
linked_authorities: Barber v Somerset County Council [2004] 1 WLR 1089
Garrett v Camden London Borough Council [2001] EWCA Civ 395

notes: CCRC reference on 1978 juvenile murder conviction; unsafe verdict due to combined Judges' Rules breaches.

enrichment.short_title: Hussain: CCRC reference quashes 1978 murder conviction after confession safeguards failures
key_facts: Abid Hussain, aged 16, was convicted in 1978 of murdering his 23-month-old brother largely on uncautioned and unrepresented admissions after nine hours in police custody.
Social Services had earlier returned the child to the family; the prosecution case depended on interviews conducted without an appropriate adult or legal advice.
A 1980 appeal failed; Hussain was later released on licence after a successful Strasbourg challenge to detention at Her Majesty's Pleasure.
The CCRC referred the case in 2003 citing combined breaches of the Judges' Rules and defective summing-up by modern standards.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal by CCRC reference under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 against a 1978 murder conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction held unsafe and quashed; the court could not determine whether another person killed the child.
enrichment.ratio: Where a juvenile's conviction rested mainly on admissions obtained without legal advice, an appropriate adult and proper cautioning, the combination of breaches gives prima facie and ultimately decisive grounds to doubt safety even in a 1978 trial, applying Bentley and Ashley King principles to modern fairness standards.
legal_issues: Whether absence of legal advice until after the second interview rendered admissions inadmissible or unreliable
Effect of interviewing a 16-year-old without an appropriate adult under 1978 Administrative Directions
Impact of uncautioned first interview on later admissions
Application of modern juvenile vulnerability standards to an old conviction

notes: Anonymised unopposed statutory demand challenge; short but complete injunction judgment.

enrichment.short_title: A Company: injunction restraining winding-up petition on disputed £320k debt
key_facts: Publishing 2000 Group served a statutory demand on the applicant company for £320,439.27 based on two invoices dated 23 December 2004.
Eversheds contended on 7 January 2005 that the debt was disputed on substantial grounds and received no response.
The company obtained an interim without-notice injunction on 14 January 2005 restraining presentation of a winding-up petition.
Detailed witness evidence showed an arguable cross-claim of about £800,000 exceeding the demanded sum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Unopposed return date application for an injunction restraining presentation of a winding-up petition based on a statutory demand.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction granted restraining Publishing 2000 from presenting a winding-up petition in reliance on the statutory demand.
enrichment.ratio: Where a debt is disputed on substantial grounds and an arguable cross-claim substantially exceeds the amount demanded, the petitioner lacks locus standi as a creditor to present a winding-up petition.
legal_issues: Whether the debt underlying the statutory demand was genuinely disputed
Effect of a substantial cross-claim on winding-up standing
Appropriateness of injunctive relief before petition presentation

notes: Committal appeal dismissed; six-week suspension extension granted before prison term takes effect.

enrichment.short_title: Messer: committal appeal dismissed with six-week suspension extension
key_facts: Mrs Messer failed to comply with possession orders for 7 Penhurst, Old Harlow dating from 2000 and 2002.
HHJ Sennitt committed her to 28 days' imprisonment for contempt on 19 January 2004, suspended until 19 July 2004 if she delivered up possession.
Multiple failed attempts to appeal the underlying possession orders delayed final resolution beyond the suspension period.
Mrs Messer challenged jurisdiction and bias but produced no viable grounds attacking the committal order itself.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a committal order for breach of a possession order, listed after earlier permission applications were dismissed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; suspension of the committal order extended for six weeks from the hearing date.
enrichment.ratio: A committal order made after long-delayed possession litigation will stand where no arguable challenge to the committal itself is advanced, but fairness may require a further short suspension to allow the contemnor to vacate before imprisonment.
legal_issues: Whether HHJ Sennitt lacked jurisdiction because committal was heard before a possession appeal was finally determined
Alleged judicial bias from the judge who made the original possession order
Whether Mrs Messer could reopen the underlying possession judgments on this appeal

notes: FSMA Part VII insurance business transfer scheme; written reasons following December 2004 sanction hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Re Allied Dunbar: court sanctions Zurich insurance business transfer scheme
key_facts: Zurich proposed transferring insurance businesses of Allied Dunbar Assurance, Zurich Assurance, COL and Pilot into Eagle Star Life Assurance.
The scheme aimed to consolidate five UK life companies into one renamed Zurich Assurance plc for efficiency and policyholder administration.
Independent Expert Mr Dumbreck reported no material reduction in security or benefit expectations for any policyholder group.
About 50 policyholders objected in writing and two made oral submissions, but the FSA approved certificates and did not attend the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written reasons following an application under section 111 FSMA to sanction an insurance business transfer scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Court satisfied statutory conditions were met and sanctioned the scheme as appropriate in all the circumstances.
enrichment.ratio: On a Part VII insurance transfer the court exercises an absolute discretion whether to sanction, giving close attention to the independent expert and FSA but deferring to directors' commercial judgment where the scheme as a whole is fair between affected classes, following Re London Life and AXA principles.
legal_issues: Whether the independent expert's appointment and reliance on company figures were sufficient
Fairness of RMM cover reductions for some policyholder groups
Impact of potential mis-selling liabilities transferred to Eagle Star
Whether policyholders were entitled to a free opt-out from the scheme

notes: Chief Master Hurst costs appeal; CFA held unenforceable for inadequate LEI enquiries in AAH referral scheme.

enrichment.short_title: Samonini v London General Transport: CFA unenforceable after inadequate LEI checks
key_facts: Mr Samonini, a taxi driver, pursued a sub-£2,000 RTA claim through Accident Advice Helpline and panel solicitors MP Jones under a CFA and ATE policy with an £798 premium.
Principal Costs Officer O'Riordan disallowed all costs because LEI enquiries before the CFA were inadequate and the CFA was unenforceable.
The solicitor relied on AAH's LEI check and did not separately ask about household or other policies before certifying no existing cover.
Chief Master Hurst reheard the appeal with fresh witness statements confirming the client had declined motor LEI cover.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under CPR 47.20 from a detailed assessment decision disallowing all claimant costs for breach of CFA Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the CFA was unenforceable and no costs were recoverable.
enrichment.ratio: Failure properly to consider under Regulation 4(2)(c) whether a client's costs risk was already insured, including by asking about relevant motor and household policies, materially adversely affects client protection where a disproportionate ATE premium was taken out, rendering the CFA unenforceable under section 58.
legal_issues: Whether AAH could delegate Regulation 4 duties to panel solicitors
Adequacy of LEI enquiries under Sarwar v Alam and Hollins v Russell
Materiality of breach where the client in fact had no LEI cover
Recoverability of ATE premium separately from CFA enforceability

notes: Rights-of-light trial; liability established but injunctions refused in favour of damages inquiry.

enrichment.short_title: Midtown v City of London Real Property: rights of light but damages not injunction
key_facts: Midtown and tenant Kendall Freeman claimed prescriptive rights of light to windows at 43 Fetter Lane threatened by the Triangle Building on the New Street Square development.
The developer argued title defects, a 1930 conveyance overriding light on yellow land, and section 237 planning override from a 1956 City acquisition.
Expert evidence showed development would reduce most rooms below the 50/50 adequate-light threshold, though offices habitually used artificial lighting.
Both claimants rejected the developer's attempts to negotiate before litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited trial on liability and entitlement to injunctive relief, with quantum of damages reserved to a later inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Rights of light established except on yellow land under the 1930 conveyance; section 237 defence rejected; injunctions refused and damages inquiries directed for both claimants.
enrichment.ratio: Where infringement of ancient lights is established but the dominant owner seeks mainly financial gain, redevelopment is likely, and the servient owner acted openly, damages may be awarded in lieu of injunction following Shelfer, Jaggard and Colls principles rather than allowing extortionate bargaining.
legal_issues: Whether Kendall Freeman acquired prescriptive rights through successive leases and section 62
Construction of the 1930 Ecclesiastical Commissioners light waiver
Whether section 237 overrides easements on land acquired in 1956 for fulfilled war-damage redevelopment
Discretionary refusal of injunction where natural light is unused and artificial lighting is standard

notes: Entry clearance adoption appeal; inability in rule 310(ix) held not to include unwillingness.

enrichment.short_title: Sharma v ECO New Delhi: gender-based rejection not inability to care under rule 310
key_facts: Radhika Sharma, an Indian girl adopted after her natural parents rejected her at birth for being female, sought entry clearance to join adoptive parents settled in the UK.
The sponsor failed to disclose the adoption when obtaining her own settlement in 1998 and the adjudicator found no genuine transfer of parental responsibility.
Both the adjudicator and IAT held paragraph 310(ix) was not satisfied because rejection was unwillingness, not inability, to care.
The child was living happily with extended family in India and doing well at school.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissing an entry clearance refusal appeal under HC 395 paragraph 310(ix) and Article 8 ECHR.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; inability does not include unwillingness and Article 8 did not require entry clearance.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 310(ix) requires adoption due to the original parents' inability, not unwillingness, to care; section 3 HRA cannot expand inability to cover voluntary gender-based rejection, and where Article 8 is not breached the Secretary of State need not grant leave outside the Rules.
legal_issues: Whether inability in paragraph 310(ix) includes unwillingness to care
Whether section 3 HRA requires a Convention-compliant reading extending inability
Whether there was a genuine transfer of parental responsibility
Application of Article 8 where family life had largely been conducted remotely
linked_authorities: Singh v Entry Clearance Officer [2005] EWCA Civ 1075
